chapter: Technique and life on the road (repeated passages)
title: From big bands to 52nd Street, Traditional Revival and tailgate style
summary: Morgenstern asks about his move to Dixieland and Sidney Bechet; Dickenson explains tailgate style and says he was a country boy who picked up the horn at home.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: Now the thing that I was interested in here intrigued me about your playing career and also that

when you left the big band things and came -- settled in New York and played -- played on 52nd Street -- around that time or a little later you had the show called Traditional Revival as Dana King. And you started playing with Sidney Bechet and the City of Paris and eventually even what you call Dixie Land.
And I guess you didn't play that style when you started, did you?
I played the style that they played at that time. At the time when they started, and that was kind of like -- sort of like Dixie Land I would say, yeah.
Was it a tail -- what they call a tailgate (inaudible).

Yeah, right. Tailgate gets me confused and I have an idea what it is but -- the word tail-gate came from the guys sitting on the back. They would sing on the back of a wagon and sit like -- so they could slide their horn you know.

There's no place to slide it and when I guess the hay rides they used to have and things like that. I think -- I listened down in New Orleans and (inaudible) which I don't believe, but however, it was practised more down there than it was because it was more people with guys with horns and things down there that had a chance to learn the horn.
Well I was a country boy and just happened to be a horn in my house so I just picked it up and start playing
